prompts: This is an instructional notebook. It introduces the conceptual foundations of linear regression by manually implementing and visualizing the model y = a * x + b on the penguins dataset, without using scikit-learn, to build intuition about the meaning of model parameters before fitting them automatically. Key learning objectives are: (1) recognizing that predicting a continuous target from a feature is a regression problem, distinguished from classification; (2) understanding that weight_flipper_length (the slope) encodes how much the predicted body mass changes per additional millimeter of flipper length — a positive value means longer flippers predict heavier penguins, a negative one the opposite; (3) understanding that intercept_body_mass shifts the line vertically and represents the theoretical predicted value when the feature is zero, even if that value is outside the data range; (4) using linear_model_flipper_mass to compute predictions for manually chosen parameter values and visualizing them against the scatterplot. Expected outputs include: a scatterplot of body mass vs. flipper length, overlaid prediction lines for several (weight, intercept) pairs including a negative-slope example, and printed body mass predictions at flipper lengths of 180 mm and 181 mm (differing by exactly weight_flipper_length grams). The flipper_length_range variable created with np.linspace is a dense synthetic grid of evenly spaced values across the observed data range, used purely to draw a smooth prediction line — it is not the original data, and passing the actual feature column would also work. Feature scaling is not required for basic linear regression on this dataset; it matters more once regularization is introduced later in the Linear Models chapter, where features on very different scales can distort the effect of the penalty term. If asked about more information on the dataset, refer to https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/trees_dataset.html
